controls.label: Radar
controls.qualification: USGS Magellan C3-MDIR synthetic color radar mosaic at 4,641 m per pixel, shown as published. The orange color is added to radar brightness; it is not measured surface color.
controls.notes: Magellan’s radar looked through the clouds from orbit. Bright ground returned more of the radar signal; dark ground returned less. USGS joined Magellan’s radar images into one global map and colored it. This is that map as USGS publishes it, at about 4.6 km per pixel, with no change to its brightness or sharpness. The orange color is added to simulate the surface. It follows radar brightness and is not measured color. Slopes facing the radar, rough ground and some minerals all look bright. The map runs from pole to pole. A flat tone fills a small area near the south pole that holds no radar image, about 0.4% of the globe.

controls.label: Elevation
controls.qualification: Magellan GTDR version 2, reprojected by USGS. Native elevation is in meters above a 6,051 km sphere. The grid spacing is about 4.64 km; radar footprints are coarser. Missing source cells remain missing.
controls.notes: Venus has no sea level to use as a baseline. This map measures height above or below a sphere with a radius of 6,051 km. Meters above the reference sphere. Negative values lie below it; positive values lie above it. Blue is lower and warm colors are higher. Magellan radar altimetry, assembled as the GTDR version 2 map and reprojected by USGS. The source grid is spaced about 4.64 km apart, but each radar measurement covers a larger area. Small terrain features are unresolved. Gray grid marks missing source data.

controls.label: Microwave emission
controls.qualification: Magellan horizontal-polarization microwave emissivity at 13 cm, adjusted for atmospheric effects. Emission angles vary from about 48° to 15°; the product is not corrected for emission angle or surface roughness. Native DN converts as (DN − 1) / 10,000.
controls.notes: Magellan measured heat emitted at a 13 cm wavelength, which passes through Venus’s clouds. Emissivity helps describe the surface’s electrical properties. A value of 1 is an ideal emitter at the same temperature and viewing angle; 0.5 emits half as much. This is a ratio, not a temperature. Magellan’s radiometer measurements were corrected for the atmosphere and unwanted antenna response. Viewing angle, roughness and surface tilt affect the result. This product does not correct all of them; one value cannot identify a rock type. Gray grid marks missing source data.

controls.label: Radar reflectivity
controls.qualification: Magellan Fresnel reflectivity from a model fit to radar echoes. It describes microwave scattering, not visible brightness or a unique composition. Native DN converts as (DN − 1) / 200.
controls.notes: The radar echo depends on the ground’s electrical properties and texture. Scientists fit an echo model to estimate Fresnel reflectivity. A dimensionless ratio: higher values mean greater reflectivity in the model. Values at or above 0.5 share the brightest color. Magellan radar echoes were fitted with a surface-scattering model. This is an inferred surface property, not the raw echo brightness. Several materials can give similar values. The map does not uniquely identify composition or show visible surface color. Gray grid marks missing source data.

controls.label: Surface roughness
controls.qualification: Magellan GSDR meter-scale surface roughness inferred from Hagfors radar-echo fits, expressed as RMS slope in degrees. This is not the slope of the elevation grid. Native DN converts as (DN − 1) / 10.
controls.notes: This describes small slopes and bumps within the area measured by radar. It helps compare smooth plains with rougher terrain. RMS slope in degrees: a measure of how much the small surface slopes vary. Higher values mean rougher ground. A Hagfors model fitted to Magellan radar echoes estimates the spread of slopes; the source calls this GSDR roughness. These are slopes at meter scales, not the slope between neighboring elevation-map cells. A 10° value is not a measured 10° hillside. Gray grid marks missing source data.

controls.label: Gravity
controls.qualification: Magellan free-air gravity from JPL model SHGJ120P to degree and order 120 (PDS MGN-V-RSS-5-GRAVITY-L2-V1.0, product RS-DMGJ120P.A01, released 1995–96 as preliminary), in mGal at the 6,051.0 km reference sphere, 1° cells.
controls.notes: How much Venus’s gravity differs from the pull of a perfectly round, evenly dense planet, at a radius of 6,051 km. Extra mass below the surface pulls harder. Milligals (mGal): 1 mGal is 0.00001 m/s², and Venus’s surface gravity is about 887,000 mGal. Red pulls harder and blue weaker; values beyond −200 or +200 mGal (0.11% of the planet, over Maxwell Montes and Atla Regio) use endpoint colors. JPL’s Magellan Gravity Science Team fitted this model to more than 3.3 million Doppler measurements of the Magellan spacecraft, 204,000 of them from Pioneer Venus Orbiter. It is the degree-120 model the archive publishes as maps; the later degree-180 model MGNP180U (Konopliv et al. 1999) is archived only as coefficients. Degree 120 resolves features about 160 km across at best, and less where Magellan flew high, near the poles and in the south. Each 1° cell holds the model value at its centre.
